rows.stem: Direction cosines of line \(\dfrac{1 - x}{0} = y = z\) are
rows.solution: A zero denominator in the symmetric form means the corresponding numerator is zero, so \(1 - x = 0\), that is \(x = 1\); the remaining part says \(y = z\). Writing the whole thing as a chain and multiplying every member by \(-1\) (which preserves the equalities) gives \(\frac{x - 1}{0} = \frac{y - 0}{-1} = \frac{z - 0}{-1}\), so the direction ratios are \(<0, -1, -1>\). Their magnitude is \(\sqrt{0 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{2}\), so dividing through gives the direction cosines \(0, \frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\). (A line has two sets of direction cosines, one for each sense along it — here the other set is \(0, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), which is not among the choices. The triples \(1, 1, 1\) and \(0, -1, -1\) cannot be direction cosines at all, since the sum of the squares must be 1 and theirs are 3 and 2.)

Test the three properties on \(R = \{(1, 3), (3, 3), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1)\}\) over \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\). Reflexive: \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\) and \((3,3)\) are all present, so R is reflexive. Symmetric: the only pair with distinct entries is \((1,3)\), and its reverse \((3,1)\) is present; the other three elements are their own reverses, so R is symmetric. Transitive: the chains to check are \((1,3)\) with \((3,3)\), needing \((1,3)\); \((1,3)\) with \((3,1)\), needing \((1,1)\); \((3,1)\) with \((1,3)\), needing \((3,3)\); and \((3,1)\) with \((1,1)\), needing \((3,1)\) — every one of these is in R, and the chains starting from \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\) or \((3,3)\) give back pairs already listed. So R is transitive as well, and hence R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \tan x & \cot x \\ -\cot x & \tan x \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A + A' = 2I\), then value of \(x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) is
rows.solution: Write down the transpose and add. With \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \tan x & \cot x \\ -\cot x & \tan x \end{bmatrix}\), we have \(A' = \begin{bmatrix} \tan x & -\cot x \\ \cot x & \tan x \end{bmatrix}\), so the off-diagonal entries cancel and \(A + A' = \begin{bmatrix} 2\tan x & 0 \\ 0 & 2\tan x \end{bmatrix} = 2\tan x \cdot I\). Setting this equal to \(2I\) gives \(\tan x = 1\). Within \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) — and excluding the endpoints, where \(\cot x\) and \(\tan x\) respectively are undefined so the matrix does not exist — the only solution is \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.solution: Differentiate \(x + y = xy\) with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on the right: \(1 + \frac{dy}{dx} = y + x\frac{dy}{dx}\). Collect the derivative terms on one side: \(1 - y = x\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{dy}{dx} = (x - 1)\frac{dy}{dx}\). Hence \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1 - y}{x - 1}\).

Rewrite the integrand in terms of sine and cosine: \(\sec x + \tan x = \frac{1}{\cos x} + \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \frac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x}\), so \(\frac{1}{\sec x + \tan x} = \frac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\). Now put \(u = 1 + \sin x\), so \(du = \cos x\,dx\) and the integral becomes \(\int\frac{du}{u} = \log|u| + C\). Hence \(\int\frac{dx}{\sec x + \tan x} = \log\left|1 + \sin x\right| + C\).

rows.stem: The general solution of the differential equation : \(x^2 dy + y^2 dx = 0\) is
rows.solution: The variables separate: \(x^2\,dy = -y^2\,dx\), so \(\frac{dy}{y^2} = -\frac{dx}{x^2}\). Integrating both sides, \(\int y^{-2}\,dy = -\int x^{-2}\,dx\) gives \(-\frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{x} + c\), that is \(-\frac{1}{y} - \frac{1}{x} = c\). Writing \(k = -c\), the general solution is \(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} = k\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the co-ordinates of the point on line \(x = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3}\) whose y co-ordinate is 3 times the \(x\) co-ordinate.
rows.solution: Set the chain equal to a parameter: \(x = \frac{y - 1}{2} = \frac{z - 2}{3} = \lambda\). Then \(x = \lambda\), \(y = 2\lambda + 1\) and \(z = 3\lambda + 2\), so a general point of the line is \(\left(\lambda,\; 2\lambda + 1,\; 3\lambda + 2\right)\). The condition is that the y-coordinate is 3 times the x-coordinate, i.e. \(2\lambda + 1 = 3\lambda\), which gives \(\lambda = 1\). Substituting back, the required point is \((1, 3, 5)\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = e^{\sin^{-1} t}\), \(y = e^{\cos^{-1} t}\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
rows.solution: Differentiate each coordinate with respect to \(t\), using the chain rule and the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = e^{\sin^{-1} t} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = e^{\cos^{-1} t} \cdot \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\). Dividing, the common factor \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\) cancels and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{e^{\cos^{-1} t}}{e^{\sin^{-1} t}} = -e^{\cos^{-1} t - \sin^{-1} t}\). At \(t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) we have \(\sin^{-1} t = \cos^{-1} t = \frac{\pi}{4}\), so the exponent is 0 and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -e^0 = -1\). (Using \(\sin^{-1} t + \cos^{-1} t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) gives the same result more quickly, since then \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -e^{\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\sin^{-1} t}\).)

Split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic plus a constant. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^2 - 4x\right) = 2x - 4\), write \(3x - 1 = A(2x - 4) + B\); comparing coefficients of \(x\) gives \(2A = 3\), so \(A = \frac{3}{2}\), and then \(-4A + B = -1\) gives \(B = 5\). Hence \(I = \frac{3}{2}\int\frac{2x - 4}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4x}}\,dx + 5\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4x}}\). For the first integral put \(u = x^2 - 4x\), so \(du = (2x - 4)dx\) and it becomes \(\frac{3}{2} \cdot 2\sqrt{u} = 3\sqrt{x^2 - 4x}\). For the second, complete the square: \(x^2 - 4x = (x - 2)^2 - 2^2\), so \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x - 2)^2 - 2^2}} = \log\left|(x - 2) + \sqrt{x^2 - 4x}\right|\). Therefore \(I = 3\sqrt{x^2 - 4x} + 5\log\left|(x - 2) + \sqrt{x^2 - 4x}\right| + C\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :

Maximize \(Z = 4500x + 5000y\)

Subject to constraints

\(x + y \leq 250\)

\(25x + 40y \leq 7000\)

\(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\)
rows.solution: First find the corner points of the feasible region. The line \(x + y = 250\) meets the axes at \((250, 0)\) and \((0, 250)\); the line \(25x + 40y = 7000\) meets them at \((280, 0)\) and \((0, 175)\). Solving the two together: from the first, \(x = 250 - y\), and substituting into the second, \(25(250 - y) + 40y = 7000\), so \(6250 + 15y = 7000\), giving \(y = 50\) and \(x = 200\). With \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\) the region is bounded, with corner points \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(250, 0)\), \(B(200, 50)\) and \(C(0, 175)\) — on the x-axis the binding constraint is \(x + y \le 250\), giving 250 rather than 280, and on the y-axis it is \(25x + 40y \le 7000\), giving 175 rather than 250. Evaluating \(Z = 4500x + 5000y\) at each corner: \(Z(O) = 0\), \(Z(A) = 11{,}25{,}000\), \(Z(B) = 9{,}00{,}000 + 2{,}50{,}000 = 11{,}50{,}000\), \(Z(C) = 8{,}75{,}000\). Hence the maximum value is \(Z = 11{,}50{,}000\), attained at \(x = 200\), \(y = 50\).

rows.stem: Find the sub-interval of \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) in which \(f(x) = \log (\sin x + \cos x)\) is increasing and decreasing.
rows.solution: On \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) both \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are positive, so \(\sin x + \cos x > 0\) and the logarithm is defined throughout. Differentiating, \(f'(x) = \frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\). Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives \(\cos x = \sin x\), i.e. \(\tan x = 1\), whose only solution in \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Since the denominator is positive on the whole interval, the sign of \(f'\) is that of \(\cos x - \sin x = \sqrt{2}\cos\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\): for \(x \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) the angle \(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\) lies in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), where the cosine is positive, so \(f'(x) > 0\); for \(x \in \left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) it lies in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\), where the cosine is negative, so \(f'(x) < 0\). Hence \(f\) is increasing on \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and decreasing on \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). (Since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single point \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\), the intervals may equally be quoted as \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\) and \(\left[\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).)

rows.stem: A rectangle of perimeter 30 cm is revolved along one of its sides to sweep out a cylinder of maximum volume. Find the dimensions of the rectangle.
rows.figure: DECORATIVE - a plain line drawing of a rectangle beside a cylinder with a rotation arrow, printed below the stem. It is unlabelled and carries no measurement; the perimeter and the axis of revolution are both stated in the text. Page idx 16. Not attached.
rows.solution: Let the sides of the rectangle be \(x\) and \(y\). The perimeter is 30 cm, so \(2(x + y) = 30\), giving \(y = 15 - x\) with \(0 < x < 15\). Revolve the rectangle about the side of length \(15 - x\); that side becomes the axis, so the cylinder swept out has height \(15 - x\) and radius \(x\). Its volume is \(V = \pi x^2 (15 - x) = \pi\left(15x^2 - x^3\right)\). Then \(\frac{dV}{dx} = \pi\left(30x - 3x^2\right) = 3\pi x(10 - x)\), which vanishes at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 10\); the value \(x = 0\) is rejected because it gives no cylinder at all, leaving \(x = 10\). Testing it, \(\frac{d^2V}{dx^2} = \pi(30 - 6x)\), and at \(x = 10\) this is \(\pi(30 - 60) = -30\pi < 0\), so the volume is indeed a maximum there. Hence \(x = 10\) and \(15 - x = 5\), so the dimensions of the rectangle are 10 cm and 5 cm. (Because \(x\) is free to take any value in \((0, 15)\), this single calculation already compares both ways of choosing the axis of revolution.)

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Find the domain of \(q(x) = \cos^{-1} (4x^2 - 3)\). Hence, find the value of \(x\) for which \(q(x) = 0\). Also, write the range of \(3q(x) - \pi\).
rows.solution:
Domain. The domain of \(\cos^{-1}\) is \([-1, 1]\), so we need \(-1 \le 4x^2 - 3 \le 1\). Adding 3 throughout gives \(2 \le 4x^2 \le 4\), so \(\frac{1}{2} \le x^2 \le 1\), that is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \le |x| \le 1\). Hence the domain of \(q\) is \(\left[-1, -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right] \cup \left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 1\right]\) — note it is a union of two intervals, since \(x = 0\) is excluded.
Solving \(q(x) = 0\). Here \(\cos^{-1}\left(4x^2 - 3\right) = 0\), so \(4x^2 - 3 = \cos 0 = 1\). Then \(4x^2 = 4\), so \(x^2 = 1\) and \(x = \pm 1\); both values lie in the domain, so \(x = 1\) or \(x = -1\).
Range of \(3q(x) - \pi\). As \(x\) runs over the domain, \(x^2\) takes every value in \(\left[\frac{1}{2}, 1\right]\), so \(4x^2 - 3\) takes every value in \([-1, 1]\) and \(q(x)\) takes every value in \([0, \pi]\), the full principal value branch of \(\cos^{-1}\). Multiplying by 3 gives \(0 \le 3q(x) \le 3\pi\), and subtracting \(\pi\) throughout gives \(-\pi \le 3q(x) - \pi \le 2\pi\). Hence the required range is \([-\pi, 2\pi]\).
